# Integration & Consolidation Strategy for a Pan-African Banking Group
## "One Group, Three Licences"

---

## 1. The core diagnostic

Multi-country bank integrations fail in five recognisable ways. All five are versions of the same mistake: treating a banking group as a single company that happens to operate in three places, when it is legally three companies that happen to share a shareholder.

**A banking licence is not a business unit.** Nigeria, Kenya and Morocco each licensed a *local legal entity* with a local board, locally accountable executives under fit-and-proper regimes, locally trapped capital and locally resident data. The CBN, CBK and Bank Al-Maghrib did not approve a group product roadmap; they approved a solvent, governable, locally-controlled bank. Any integration plan that assumes you can run these as branches of a single balance sheet is not aggressive — it is unlicensed.

**Core-banking migration is the highest-variance activity in banking, and it is almost never the source of the synergy.** Big-bang core replacements have destroyed more shareholder value in this sector than any strategic error. The cost synergy from "one core" is real but small, arrives in year five, and is dwarfed by the downside of a single failed cutover: deposit flight, regulatory sanction, and the permanent loss of the local management team who could have fixed it. **Cores are the last thing you consolidate, not the first.**

**Capital and cash are not fungible; capabilities are.** Nigerian naira faces recapitalisation obligations and repatriation friction. The dirham sits behind Office des Changes controls. Kenya is the most open of the three and will still not tolerate a subsidiary being funded as a group cash-pool node. Any thesis built on upstreaming Nigerian profits into Moroccan growth is a fantasy. **Plan every subsidiary as self-funding and self-capitalising; extract group value through capability transfer, funding cost, corridor revenue and financial-crime scale — not treasury sweeps.**

**Entrenched local management is not an obstacle to the deal; it *is* the deal.** The relationship managers hold the corporate deposits. The local CEO holds the supervisory relationship. In markets where lending is relationship-collateralised and deposit concentration is high, replacing the top 100 people destroys the asset you bought. But leaving them fully autonomous means you own three banks and a logo.

**Data does not travel, so the group must be built on models and schemas, not on a central warehouse of customer records.** Nigeria's data-protection regime plus CBN localisation expectations, Kenya's Data Protection Act and ODPC, and Morocco's CNDP framework will not be reconciled by a group-wide cloud tenant in Ireland. Design for that constraint from day one or rebuild in year three.

**The resolution: hold the *control plane* and the *data contract* constant; let the *core systems, the product catalogue, the experience shell, the brand and the commercial motion* vary — on a published convergence schedule with hard caps on permanent divergence.**

---

## 2. Six-layer architecture, with a divergence cap

| Layer | Contents | Variation policy |
|---|---|---|
| **L0 — Group control plane (invariant)** | Risk appetite & credit policy framework, capital/liquidity policy, financial-crime standards (KYC/AML/sanctions/screening thresholds), model governance, cybersecurity baseline, engineering platform, chart-of-accounts spine, incident and operational-resilience standard | **Zero forks.** One standard, three implementations |
| **L1 — Customer/product ontology** | Canonical customer, product, transaction and exposure model + per-supervisor **reporting overlays** (CBN, CBK, BAM/AMMC, IFRS) | Data, not code. One overlay per supervisor |
| **L2 — Local product catalogue** | Rates, fees, tenors, collateral rules, local credit scorecards, participative/Islamic products, agency-banking terms | Fully local, group-approved risk parameters |
| **L3 — Experience shell** | Channel mix (app / USSD / agent / branch), language (EN + Pidgin; EN + Swahili; Arabic + French), onboarding flow, mobile-money integration, comms tone | **Experience Packs** — declarative config |
| **L4 — Trust envelope** | Licence conditions, data residency, consumer protection, outsourcing/cloud approvals, complaint handling, sharia governance board (Morocco), breach reporting | Per country, legally reviewed |
| **L5 — Commercial motion** | Brand, segment focus, distribution partnerships, pricing posture, sales model | Per market |
| **L‑1 — Legacy cores** | Three incumbent core-banking systems | **Treated as replaceable substrate beneath L1, never as the group system of record** |

### The Divergence Ledger

Every local exception is classified *before* work starts:

- **Class C — Configuration.** Expressed as parameter, policy value or feature flag. **Target ≥85% of all local requests.**
- **Class E — Extension.** A plug-in at a published seam: core adapter, payment-rail connector (NIBSS/NIP, PesaLink & M-Pesa, GIM-UEMOA/domestic switch, PAPSS), national-ID/BVN verification, regulatory-report generator. The *interface* must be reusable even if the implementation serves one country.
- **Class F — Fork.** Divergent core logic, schema or control standard. Requires Group Integration Board approval, a named owner, a **sunset date**, and a merge-back plan. **Hard cap: three live forks across the group.**

Two supporting rules. Nothing enters L0 unless it serves **two or more countries** or is a supervisory requirement. Any Class F item open at its sunset date is merged, generalised into a Class C capability, or the local feature is withdrawn.

---

## 3. The single most important design decision: the Group Data Contract

Build **one canonical ontology** for customer, account, product, transaction, exposure and counterparty — and treat every supervisor's reporting taxonomy as an **overlay** mapping official codes to canonical objects.

Then split the estate physically:

- **Local data planes** (one per country, in-country residency) hold raw customer records, transactions and PII. Nothing leaves.
- **Group control plane** consumes only conformed **aggregates, pseudonymised features and model artefacts** — never raw records.
- **Risk and pricing models use shared priors and local posteriors.** A Kenyan SME repayment signal improves the structure of the group's SME scorecard used in Lagos and Casablanca, without a single customer record crossing a border. Calibration is always local; architecture is always shared.
- **Reporting renders in local codes.** The CBN sees CBN returns; BAM sees BAM returns; the group sees IFRS consolidation. Same underlying object, three renderings, one reconciliation.

Consequences worth stating: consolidated risk, group financial crime, and single-customer-view per country all become achievable **without core migration**, which is precisely why core migration can be deferred. This layer is the actual acquisition thesis. Build it first.

---

## 4. Sequencing: control → connect → converge → consolidate

> **Two absolute ordering rules.**
> **(1) Never migrate a core and rebrand the same bank within the same 12 months.**
> **(2) Never run two core migrations concurrently anywhere in the group.**

| Wave | Window | What happens | What deliberately does *not* |
|---|---|---|---|
| **W0 — Stabilise & ring-fence** | Day 1–100 | Retain top 100 people; confirm boards & fit-and-proper filings; supervisory introductions in all three capitals; freeze the local roadmaps you don't understand yet; forensic view of capital, liquidity, NPLs, related-party exposures, sanctions backlog; Nigeria recapitalisation plan filed | No rebrand, no system change, no headcount announcement |
| **W1 — Control plane** | M3–12 | Group CRO/CFO standards live; unified credit policy framework; financial-crime screening consolidated onto one engine with local hosting; chart-of-accounts mapping; consolidated close from 45 days to 10; cyber baseline; Divergence Ledger operating | No customer-facing change |
| **W2 — Connect (hollow the core)** | M9–24 | API/integration fabric per country; single customer view per country; group digital channel stack rolled out country-by-country on top of legacy cores; local data planes live; group product factory for new products only | Legacy cores untouched; existing products not re-platformed |
| **W3 — Converge (revenue synergies)** | M18–36 | Corridor products: intra-African trade finance, diaspora remittance (Morocco–Europe, Nigeria–UK/US, Kenya–Gulf), PAPSS/AfCFTA settlement, group cash management for multinationals; consolidated card issuing & processing; group treasury desk services (not cash pooling); shared engineering and procurement | Still no core migration |
| **W4 — Consolidate (selective core replacement)** | M30–54 | Replace a core **only** where an independent trigger exists — vendor end-of-life, capacity ceiling, supervisory finding, or unsustainable run-cost. Sequence: lowest-risk balance sheet first, one at a time, with a proven rollback and a parallel-run period. Some cores may never be replaced | No simultaneous migrations; no migration in a market under deposit stress |
| **W5 — Brand & organisational convergence** | M48+ | Masterbrand where the economics justify it; shared service centres; legal-entity simplification where permitted | Nothing forced on a market that fails the brand gate |

**Why W3 precedes W4:** corridor revenue is the only synergy that is both large and unavailable to the standalone banks. It requires the *data contract* and the *channel layer*, not a common core. Delivering it in year two funds patience in year four and — critically — proves to local management and to supervisors that the group adds something.

---

## 5. Brand: an endorsed ladder with gates, not a date

Brand consolidation is a *deposit-risk* decision disguised as a marketing decision. Use a test, not a timetable.

**Gate criteria for advancing a market up the ladder:**

1. Unaided awareness and trust of the local brand vs. the group brand in that market
2. Deposit concentration — share of deposits from the top 20 depositors, and their stated brand sensitivity
3. Supervisory posture on a name change (materiality, re-papering, licence conditions)
4. Cost of change: cards, signage, contracts, KYC/consent re-papering, switch and scheme registrations
5. **Twelve clean months since the last major systems change in that market**

**The ladder:**

| Stage | Form | Typical trigger |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | *LocalBank* (unchanged) + discreet "part of [Group]" endorsement | Day 1, all markets |
| 2 | *LocalBank, a [Group] bank* — co-branded, group visual system, group digital app | Control plane live + 12 stable months |
| 3 | *[Group] LocalName* transitional lock-up | Corridor products live; deposit base stable through a rate/FX cycle |
| 4 | *[Group]* masterbrand | Only where 1–5 all clear |

**Expected asymmetry.** A market where the acquired brand is weak, the customer base is young and digital, and the group brand signals stability may reach St
